name: Prusa Research a.s.
origin_detail: Founded in Prague in 2012 by Josef Prusa, a RepRap core developer whose Prusa Mendel / Prusa i3 RepRap designs the company first sold as kits; grew from a one-person start-up to 1,000+ staff without disclosed outside funding.
openness_notes: Initial 3: i3 designs up to the MK3 were published as GPL OpenSCAD code, firmware GPL, slicer AGPL (no complete BOM ever published, so not 4; governance is corporate). From the MK4 (2023) printable parts were released only as STLs and the Nextruder/xBuddy board design files withheld; schematics published but PCB manufacturing layouts withheld 'to avoid untested clone boards'. CORE One/CORE One L frame CAD released Dec 2025 under Prusa's own Open Community License (OCL), which forbids selling machines or commercial remixes without a separate agreement, so it is source-available rather than open hardware. Firmware stays GPL and PrusaSlicer AGPL-3.0. Current = 2 (software/firmware open, current hardware designs only under a non-open licence, older models open).

risk_events: 2023-03: Prusa blog cites 1:1 commercial clones, stripped copyright headers and local patents filed on open-source work
2023: MK4 launched with design files withheld (STL only); PCB layouts withheld to avoid clone boards
2024-11: CORE One announced as closed hardware; Hackaday: 'Prusa's open source hardware dream quietly dies'
2025-08: Josef Prusa post 'open hardware desktop 3D printing is dead' blames below-cost Chinese printers and state-reimbursed Chinese patent filings
2026-03: first-ever layoffs, about 70 non-production roles of about 1,144, as sales targets were missed
Competitive pressure from closed Bambu Lab, whose Bambu Studio slicer derives from Prusa's open PrusaSlicer
robustness: Founder-controlled and bootstrapped (no disclosed outside funding), profitable but thin 2024 net margin (CZK 47.3M net on CZK 3.65B revenue); vertically integrated (Prusament filament, Printables community site) with a Delaware factory (Prusa USA, formerly Printed Solid, renamed July 2026) serving a market that is about 35% of revenue. Its open software (PrusaSlicer) is widely forked, so that part would outlive the company.
physical_science_relevance: RepRap-lineage open FFF printers are a standard tool for fabricating custom labware and open scientific hardware; GPL-era i3 designs remain reusable by labs, while OCL designs allow lab use and spare parts but not commercial resale.
openness_effect_assessment: Open GPL designs and the RepRap community gave Prusa fast, cheap brand growth from a one-person start-up to roughly CZK 3.65B revenue (2024) with no disclosed outside capital. From 2023 the company progressively withheld hardware files, citing 1:1 clones and Chinese patent filings, yet Hackaday notes the feared Prusa clones are hard to find; the bigger competitive threat became closed, subsidised Chinese printers (Bambu Lab) that reused Prusa's open slicer. Closing did not prevent slowing sales and the first layoffs in 2026, suggesting price competition rather than cloning was the binding constraint.
key_takeaway: Prusa is the clearest case of an open-hardware pioneer retreating to 'open software, source-available hardware': it kept firmware (GPL) and slicer (AGPL) open but moved its newest printers' CAD to a custom non-commercial Open Community License. Openness built the brand and community cheaply, but it did not protect against well-funded closed competitors, and the protective licence came after market share had already shifted.

hardware_extras.patents: In March 2023 Josef Prusa wrote that Prusa would 'never consider patenting' its open-source contributions, while complaining of others patenting open work; the Aug 2025 post cites rapid growth of Chinese 3D-printing patent filings (Espacenet chart). No Prusa patent filings were verified in these searches.
hardware_extras.clone_impacts: Prusa cites 1:1 commercial clones and withholds PCB layouts to avoid untested clone boards; Hackaday (2024) disputes how many Prusa clones exist. The larger documented reuse is software: PrusaSlicer forked into Bambu Studio and others.
